a) Serial number of the case : 4579/2019 b) Date of commission of : 15.04.2017  Offence c) Name of the complainant : Sh. Anoop d) Name, parentage and address : Sukhbir Singh @ Jimmy, S/o Sh.st  of the accused Jaspal Singh, R/o H.No. G-1  243/244, Madangir, New Delhi.
e) Offence complained of : 279/337/304A IPC f) Plea of the accused : Accused pleaded not guilty g) Final order : Acquittal h) Date of final order : 04.01.2024  BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS FOR THE DECISION CASE OF THE PROSECUTION 1. On 15.04.2017, at about 10:30 pm, at the time when complainant Anoop was letting the vehicles get parked in parking and his father was sleeping on floor near the parking entry, the accused Jimmy came in rash and negligent manner, in high speed on vehicle bearing registration no.
DL1RTA4012 (make Swift Dezire, white in colour) from NBCC Plaza side to BRT Road and he suddenly took left turn due to which his vehicle lost control and it ran over his father resulting into injuries to his father. The complainant along with his associates shifted his father in the vehicle of accused Jimmy to Madan Mohan Malviya Hospital and after treatment, his father got discharged. 
On the night of 15.04.2017, due to extreme pain, his father was admitted in Safdarjung Hospital,

1 however for better treatment, complainant admitted his father to Loknayak Hospital where he got treated and his MLC was prepared. During treatment, Ramesh expired. 
2. Subsequently, the FIR was registered against the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 279/337/304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter referred to as "the IPC"). 
NOTICE 3. Vide order dated 02.11.2022, notice for the offences punishable under Sections 279/337/304A IPC was framed against the accused, who pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 
ADMISSION/DENIAL OF DOCUMENTS 4. Vide order dated 15.12.2022, in compliance to the provisions of Section 294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter "the Code"), the accused admitted the genuineness of; i)
Endorsement by DO; ii) FIR No. 164 /2017; iii) Certificate U/S 65B Indian Evidence Act; iv) MLC No. EED/1578 dated 16.04.2017 of deceased prepared by Dr. Manish; v) Death summary report dated 17.04.2017 of deceased prepared by Dr. Sachin Chaudhary ; vi) PM No. 318/2017 report of deceased prepared by Dr. Utkarsh ; vii) Examination report no. C-693/2017 dated 25.07.2017 by Dr.
Kanaklata Verma ; viii) Histopathological report no. 20/2017 dated 19.09.2017 by Dr. Abhishek Yadav; ix) DD No. 3B dated 16.04.2017 and x) Mechanical Inspection Report of vehicle bearing No.
DL-1RTA-4012 vide Ex. A1 to A10.
EVIDENCE OF THE PROSECUTION 5. Prosecution has examined seven witnesses i.e. PW1 Sh. Anoop (the complainant), PW2 Abhishek,
PW3 HC Balkar, PW4 HC Rajesh Kumar, PW5 Balwant Kumar, PW6 SI Rajdeep (the Investigating Officer) and PW7 Inspector Jitender Malik. 
6. PW1 Anoop (complainant) deposed that at the time of incident, he along with his father, mother and brother Abhishek, were residing and also working in SDMC parking, Sector 4, Pushp Vihar as they did not have any other residence in Delhi. On 15.04.2017, at about 10:30 pm, when he was getting vehicles parked in parking and his father was lying near entry gate of parking, at that time the accused in his car (make white Swift Dezire) bearing no. DL1RTA4012 came from NBCC Plaza road side, in very high speed and in rash and negligent manner with speed of 60-80 kmph. While driving so, the accused took turn towards parking and ran over the car over the father of PW1 and his car dragged the deceased to a distance of 30-40 feet. The accused regularly used to park his vehicle there and he alleged that accused knew that his father used to lie near the entry gate. 
Thereafter, PW1 shouted and 3-4 persons gathered there with the help of whom PW1 took out his father from beneath the car. He alleged that there was sufficient space to enter the parking and he should not have turned his car in such speed. The deceased was then shifted to Madan Mohan Malviya Hospital in car of accused and his mother also accompanied them. Being frightened, the mother of PW1 informed the doctors that the deceased fell from stairs and sustained injuries. After giving primary medical aid to father of PW1, he got discharged and they returned to parking. At State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
2 about 12:00 midnight -01:00 am, his father started feeling pain in whole body and they shifted his father to Safdarjung Hospital , however doctors at Safdarjung Hospital refused to admit him and suggested to admit his father to Lok Nayak JPNA Hospital for proper treatment. Thereafter, they went to said hospital and admitted his father there and police officials also reached there and inquired PW1 regarding the incident and IO prepared site plan on his instance. On 17.04.2017,
father of PW1 was declared dead and postmortem was done after identification by PW1 and his brother and then deadbody was handed over to them. He deposed that no CCTV camera was installed at the parking. The witness correctly identified the accused. The witness was duly cross- examined. 
7. PW2 Abhishek deposed that in the year 2017, he was residing in abovementioned parking along with my family (i.e. PW1, mother Sarita Devi and father/deceased Ramesh). On 15.04.2017, when he was in the parking and his father was sleeping near the entrance of the parking, at about 10:30 PM,
the accused Jimmy who was known to PW2 prior to 15.04.2017, had reached from the side of BRT in his car bearing No. DL1RTA4012 (make Maruti Swift Dezire white in colour), at a high speed in a negligent manner and he took left turn, the car had gone out of his control and ran over the car on his father. Thereafter, when they heard the noise of his father, he reached there and picked up his father with the help of others and shifted him to Madan Mohan Hospital in the car of accused. After some bandage, doctor discharged him and they returned home. Thereafter, on the same night, when his father started shouting due of pain, they had taken him to Safdarjung Hospital and then to Lok Nayak Hospital for treatment where he died. After identification of deadbody, identification memo was prepared and after the post mortem, deadbody was handed over to PW1 and PW2. Witness has correctly identified the accused. Witness also correctly identified the alleged car in the photographs shown to him. The witness was duly cross examined. 
8. PW3 HC Balkar deposed that on 18.04.2017, he joined the investigation along with IO SI Rajdeep and they reached at the spot (i.e. parking, Sector 4, Pushp Vihar, Saket) where they met the complainant Anoop and IO prepared site plan at his instance. Thereafter, PW3 along with IO reached at LNJP Hospital where postmortem of deceased Ramesh got conducted and deadbody of the deceased Ramesh was handed over to his family and they came back to PS. The accused Sukhbir @ Jimmy reached PS where after interrogation, he was arrested. As the offence was bailable,
accused was released on bail. Accused also produced the offending vehicle i.e. Swift Dezire car,
white in colour bearing no. DL1RTA4012, his original DL and original RC of offending vehicle and other photocopy of documents pertaining to the offending vehicle which were seized by IO. Witness correctly identified the accused. The witness also correctly identified photographs of alleged vehicle. 
The witness was duly cross examined. 
9. PW4 HC Rajesh Kumar deposed that on 07.06.2017, IO handed over to him a forwarding letter along with sealed exhibits for depositing the same to FSL Chanakyapuri and he deposited the same to FSL Chanakyapuri and took acknowledgment from FSL and also deposited the same with MHC(M). He further deposed that on 31.07.2017, IO handed over to him an authority letter to collect the FSL result. Thereafter, he collected the same from FSL Chanakyapuri and deposited it with MHC(M). During his custody, no tampering has been done with the sealed exhibits and sealed FSL result. The witness was duly cross- examined.

3 10. PW5 Sh. Balwant Kumar deposed that he is a driver by profession and on 15.04.2017 at about 10:30 pm, he went to a dhaba, near abovementioned MCD parking, Sector 4, Pushp Vihar near BRT corridor and was getting his food packed. At that time, he witnessed that the accused Jimmy was carrying the injured Panditji/parking attendant in his car (make Swift Dezire) bearing no.
DL1RTA4012 and he also accompanied them in said car to hospital. He deposed that while they were on the way to hospital, he came to know that the accident with injured occurred due to negligent driving of accused. Then, he returned to his house. Witness correctly identified the accused. The witness also correctly identified the photographs of offending vehicle. The witness was duly cross examined. 
11. PW6 SI Rajdeep deposed on 17.04.2017, he was on emergency duty when SI Ashish Sharma from PS Sadar Bazar came to PS and handed over one MLC of injured Ramesh s/o Shiv Dayal and one statement of his son. Thereafter, he along with Ct Balkar went to the LNJP hospital where injured Ramesh was under treatment and unfit for statement and at that time, his family was also not there.
Subsequently, he with Ct Balkar reached Sector 4, Pushp Vihar, Saket where they tried to find the eyewitnesses or family members of injured but nobody was there so they returned to PS. After sometime PW1 went to PS, gave his statement, upon which the rukka was prepared and the same was handed over to DO for registration of FIR. 
After registration of FIR, DO handed over the copy of FIR and original rukka to PW6 for further investigation. At about 10:30 pm, he received information from LNJP Hospital regarding death of injured Ramesh during treatment. On 18.04.2017, he along with Ct Balkar reached Sector 4, Pushp Vihar parking where he met PW1 and on his instance, site plan was prepared. He recorded the statement of other eyewitnesses. Thereafter, he with Ct Balkar reached at MAMC Hospital where the postmortem of the deceased got conducted and then dead body of deceased was handed over to his family members. PW6 also recorded statements of family members of deceased for identification of deadbody of Ramesh. The doctor handed over exhibits including Viscera, histopath contents of the deceased which were seized by PW6 and he returned to PS and deposited the exhibits in malkhana. The notice u/s 133 MV Act was served upon the accused for vehicle no. DL1RTA4012 (make white Swift Dezire) and accused Sukhbir Singh @ Jimmy along with offending vehicle went to PS and replied on notice. The offending vehicle, DL of accused, RC,
photocopy of insurance, permit, badge and fitness of offending vehicle were seized. 
After interrogation, accused was arrested. As the offence was bailable, the accused was released on bail. During investigation, PW6 got mechanical inspection of offending vehicle conducted. On 12.08.2017, he prepared panchnama of superdari of offending vehicle. He also recorded the statement of witnesses u/s 161 CrPC and Viscera was sent to FSL and histopath contents were sent to AIIMS for examination. 
As PW6 got transferred from PS Saket , he submitted the file with MHCR. The witness correctly identified the offending vehicle in photographs shown to him. The witness was duly cross examined.

4 12. PW7 Inspector Jitender Malik deposed that on 14.02.2019, the investigation of present case was marked to him upon which he read the file and obtained the subsequent opinion upon nature of injuries from Maulana Azad Medical College and he compiled the documents of the case and filed the charge-sheet in present case. The witness was duly cross examined. 
STATEMENT / DEFENCE OF THE ACCUSED 13. In his statement recorded under Section 313 of the Code, the accused stated that on 15.04.2017,
he was driving the aforesaid taxi and when he was going to the parking lot to park his vehicle, he saw deceased lying on the ground right after entry of parking lot. He then asked reason to the son of deceased to which he stated that the deceased had fallen from foot over bridge. He took the deceased with his son (one Tannu, name he cannot clearly recollect) and his wife to hospital. He stated that he was not driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner. In MLC, it is stated that the deceased fell from stairs and had taken alcohol. He stated that he is innocent and has been falsely implicated in this case. Accused did not lead any evidence in his defence. 
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS 14. The record has been thoroughly and carefully perused. The respective submissions of Sh. Naresh Choudhary, Ld. Assistant Public Prosecutor for State and Sh. Pawan Kumar, Ld. Counsel for the accused have been considered. 
15. In order to establish an offence punishable under Section 279 of the IPC, it must be shown that the accused was driving the vehicle on a public road in a rash or negligent way, threatening human life or likely to cause harm or injury to another person. Where an offence under Section 279 is established, the accused is also culpable under Section 304A of the IPC where his rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide causes death of any person. Therefore, the main ingredients which need to be established beyond reasonable doubt by the prosecution are:
a) Firstly, that the accused was driving the vehicle on a public road;
b) Secondly, that the accused was driving the vehicle in a rash or negligent manner so as to endanger human life; and;
c) Thirdly, that death has been caused due to the said conduct of the accused. 
16. The accused has admitted that he was driving the alleged offending vehicle No. DL-1RTA-4012 on the date of the incident. He has also admitted that he was at the site of the incident at the time of the incident. The accused, in his statement under Section 294 of the Code has admitted the genuineness of the MLC No. EED/1578 dated 16.04.2017 of deceased prepared by Dr. Manish (Ex.
A4), Death Summary Report dated 17.04.2017 of deceased prepared by Dr. Sachin Chaudhary (Ex.
A5), Post Mortem No. 318/2017 of deceased prepared by Dr. Utkarsh (Ex. A6), Examination Report No. C-693/2017 dated 25.07.2017 by Dr. Kanaktala Verma (Ex. A7) and Histopathological report no.
20/2017 dated 19.09.2017 by Dr. Abhishek Yadav (Ex. A8) have been admitted by the accused. The State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
5 post mortem report has clearly concluded that the death is due to rib cage fracture caused by blunt force trauma indicating that the collision of the offending vehicle on the deceased victim could have caused the death of the deceased victim. Therefore, it is established that the victim passed away on account of the injuries which appear to have been suffered due to a road accident. However, the point of contention in the present case is whether the offending vehicle was being driven by the accused in a rash or negligent manner and that the accused caused the death of the victim due to such driving. 
17. Therefore, the only question remaining to be proved by the prosecution is that the accused was driving the offending vehicle in a rash or negligent manner and that such driving has caused death of the victim. The Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that the testimony of the prosecution witnesses is replete with various inadequacies and therefore, the prosecution case has not been established beyond reasonable doubt.
18. On perusal of the file and the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses, the following deficiencies in the prosecution version and inconsistencies and contradictions in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses are found:
a ) The incident is dated 15.04.2017. It is stated in the chargesheet that the deceased victim was lying on the ground near the entry gate of the parking. It is further stated that the accused took a turn towards the parking while driving the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent manner and consequently, the offending vehicle ran over the victim. The first question which crops up is as to why the deceased victim was lying on the ground near the parking gate. PW1 Anoop has tried to cover up this lapse on behalf of the deceased victim by stating that the accused was aware that his father (the deceased victim) used to lie there near the gate. However, despite said explanation, the conduct of the deceased victim in lying on the ground near the parking gate cannot be condoned as it is not expected of a reasonable man to lie on the ground when it is expected that vehicles will turn towards the parking lot for parking the vehicle. Can the accused be blamed for the negligent conduct of the deceased victim? The answer is definitely in the negative. 
b) Secondly, in the MLC dated 16.04.2017, it has been mentioned that the victim fell from the stairs. On this point, specific questions were asked in the cross-examination by the Ld. Counsel for accused. PW1 Anoop (son of the deceased victim) stated that his mother gave the said statement regarding the nature of injuries to the doctor as she was frightened. This inconsistency also enures to the benefit of the accused. 
c) Thirdly, the Ld. Counsel for accused has argued that there is a slight elevation near the entry to the parking and therefore, the victim would not have been visible to the accused. PW6 SI Rajdeep has admitted that there is a ramp at the entrance of the parking. PW2 Abhishek also admitted in his cross-examination that there is a ramp before entering the parking and one has to use the said ramp to enter inside the parking. He has also admitted that the deceased victim was sleeping on the lower State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
6 slope of the ramp and was drunk at that time. In this background, it is reasonable to assume that as there was a ramp and the victim was lying on the lower slope of the ramp, it cannot be expected of a prudent driver to notice or assume that some person will be lying on the end of the ramp. This further fortifies the fact that the incident did not happen on account of negligence of the accused and was in fact, on account of the negligence of the victim. Also, the authenticity of the site plan (Ex. PW1/B) is questionable as it does not indicate the ramp or the elevation though existence of said ramp is admitted by the IO himself. 
d) Fourthly, PW2 Abhishek in his examination in chief did not depose that the vehicle was being driven rashly or negligently by the accused. In his re-examination by the Ld. APP for State, he deposed that the accused was driving the vehicle rashly. Also,
there is contradiction in the depositions of the PWs as PW1 has deposed that the victim was not in an alcoholic condition at the time of the incident. However, PW2 Abhishek has deposed that the victim had consumed alcohol at the time of the incident. These contradictions attune to the benefit of the accused. 
e) Fifthly, PW2 Abhishek deposed that in addition to himself and PW1 Anoop, one Saroj Tiwari and his brother Vinod Tiwari were present. However, PW1 deposed that one rehdiwala Manish and one Bunty were present. Therefore, both the witnesses have given contrary deposition w.r.t. the persons who were present at the spot at the time of the incident. The IO has not joined all the aforesaid persons in the investigation. The only other public witness is PW5 Balwant Kumar who was not an eye witness to the incident and therefore, has not deposed anything w.r.t. rashness or negligence of the accused. The IO, by not joining all the independent witnesses, has prejudiced the case of the prosecution. 
19. This Court is cognizant that minor inconsistencies should not tantamount to substantial prejudice of the complainant [Ref:
Bharwada Bhoginibhai Hirjibhai vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983 SC 753) wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that "Too much importance cannot be attached to minor discrepancies and a witness cannot be expected to possess a photographic memory to recall the details of an incident". However, the contradictions and inconsistencies listed above cannot be said to be minor when viewed cumulatively. In fact, the said inconsistencies have incurably led to complete failure of the prosecution's case. 
20. Further, on the question whether the accused was driving the offending vehicle in a rash or negligent manner, the factum of rashness and negligence has to be gathered from the surrounding circumstances. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ravi Kapoor vs. State of Rajasthan [Crl. Appeal No.
1838/2009] inter alia held as under:
"10. In order to examine the merit or otherwise of contentions State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
7 (b) and (c) raised on behalf of the appellant, it is necessary for the Court to first and foremost examine (a) what is rash and negligent driving; and (b) whether it can be gathered from the attendant circumstances. Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case. It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation. It must be examined in light of the attendant circumstances. A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result. It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently. Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct. Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to 'rash and negligent driving' within the meaning of the language of Section 279 IPC. That is why the legislature in its wisdom has used the words 'manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life'. The preliminary conditions, thus, are that (a)
it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life. Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted. 
11. 'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do. Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one;
it is rather a comparative term. It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case. 
Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court. In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence. 
12. The Court has to adopt another parameter, i.e., 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence. The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrian happen to be children of tender years. It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians. They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others. 
13. The other principle that is pressed in aid by the courts in such cases is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur. This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence. Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
8 but cannot prove how the accident occurred. The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record. The Act itself contains a provision which concerns with the consequences of driving dangerously alike the provision in the IPC that the vehicle is driven in a manner dangerous to public life. Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act. The courts have also taken the concept of 'culpable rashness' and 'culpable negligence' into consideration in cases of road accidents. 'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening. The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria). 'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness. The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection. In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence. This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct. [Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988' (First Edition, 2010]." 
21. Rash or negligent driving has to be seen from the attendant circumstances. The only question to be seen is whether the said injuries were caused by the reckless and negligent driving of the accused. 
A rash and negligent act has been described by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mohammed Aynuddin @ Miyan vs. State of Andhra Pradesh [(2000) 7 Supreme Court Cases 72] in the following words:
"A rash act is primarily an over hasty act. It is opposed to a deliberate act. Still a rash act can be a deliberate act in the sense that it was done without due care and caution. 
Culpable rashness lies in running the risk of doing an act with recklessness and with indifference as to the consequences. Criminal negligence is the failure to exercise duty with reasonable and proper care and precaution guarding against injury to the public generally or to any individual in particular. It is the imperative duty of the driver of a vehicle to adopt such reasonable and proper care and precaution."
22. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Guljeet Singh Kochar and Others vs. The State [121 (2005)
DLT 516] examined the facts essential to hold a man guilty under Section 304A IPC and held as under:
".... The offence cannot be presumed merely because of an unfortunate incident... 
... In order to establish criminal liability, facts must be such that the negligence of the accused prima facie show utter disregard to life and safety of others so as to amount to crime. The words 'rashly or negligently' are distinguishable, sometimes overlapping...

9 These principles have been reiterated by Supreme Court in several decisions including the following:
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 
.............................................................................. 
(ii) In Suleman Rehiman Mulani v. State of Maharashtra (supra), the accused was charged for rash and negligent driving with only a learner's license. It was held:
"The requirements of this section are that the death of any person must have been caused by the accused by doing any rash or negligent act. In other words, there must be proof that the rash or negligent act of the accused was the proximate cause of the death. There must be direct nexus between the death of a person and the rash or negligent act of the accused." 
............................................................................. ............................................................................. 
6. Black's Law Dictionary (Sixth Edition) defines 'criminal negligence' as under:
"Criminal negligence which will render killing a person manslaughter is the omission on the part of the person to do some act which an ordinarily careful and prudent man would do under like circumstances, or the doing of some act which an ordinarily careful, prudent man under like circumstances would not do by reason of which another person is endangered in life or bodily safety; the word 'ordinary' being synonymous with 'reasonable' in this connection. 
Negligence of such a character, or occurring under such circumstances, as to be punishable as a crime by statute; or (at common law) such a flagrant and reckless disregard of the safety of others, or willful indifference to the injury liable to follow,
as to convert an act otherwise lawful into a crime when it results in personal injury or death."
23. The prosecution witnesses have deposed that the victim was lying on the ground near the entry gate of the parking. The said conduct of the victim itself absolves the liability of the accused, if any. 
Moreover, the other inconsistencies and contradictions highlighted above, also create aspersions as to whether the accused was driving the offending vehicle in a rash or negligent manner. There are no other public witnesses (who are not family members of the victim) who have been examined. The site plan also does not confirm the version of the prosecution witnesses w.r.t. existence of a ramp. 
The eye witnesses who ought to have established that the offending vehicle was being driven in a rash or negligent manner, have miserably failed to do so. Their depositions are not credible and benefit accordingly, must ensure to the accused. There is an absolute dearth of evidence regarding rashness or negligence in the manner in which the accused was driving the vehicle as the deposition of public witnesses qua said fact is absent. 
State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
10 24. The evidence in this case is too scanty and inconsistent to fasten the accused with criminal negligence. Some credible and reliable evidence is indispensably needed to presume that the victim was behaving prudently while the accused acted negligently while driving the offending vehicle. 
Such further evidence is lacking in this case. Therefore, the court is disabled from concluding that the accused was driving his vehicle rashly or negligently. The corollary thereof is that the conviction of the appellant of the offence is unsustainable. 
25. Thus, having considered the testimonies of the witnesses and the documents on record, it is absolutely clear that the prosecution does not bring home the element of rashness or negligence that is an essential ingredient to establish offences under Sections 279 and 304A of IPC. Needless to say,
that the burden to prove the guilt of accused is on prosecution and this general burden never shifts. 
Hence, in view of the foregoing discussion, it is held that the prosecution has failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the accident causing demise of the victim namely Sh. Ramesh Chand was caused by the accused due to his rash or negligent driving of the taxi bearing no. DL-1RTA-4012. 
The evidence led by prosecution is deficient and inconsistent and therefore, does not inspire the confidence of this Court. Accused Sukhbir Sigh @ Jimmy S/o Sh Jaspal Singh is thus acquitted of the offences punishable under Sections 279/337/304A IPC in the present case. 
26. Bail bond in compliance of Section 437A of the Code is directed to be furnished. 
Dictated and announced in open Court on 04.01.2024.

annotations.text: Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case.
It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
It must be examined in light of the attendant circumstances.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.
Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to 'rash and negligent driving' within the meaning of the language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the legislature in its wisdom has used the words 'manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life'.

The preliminary conditions, thus, are that (a)
it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted.

11. 'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.

Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one;
it is rather a comparative term.
It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.

Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.
In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence.
12. The Court has to adopt another parameter, i.e., 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.

The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrian happen to be children of tender years.

It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others.
13. The other principle that is pressed in aid by the courts in such cases is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.

This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.

Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident State vs Sukhbir Singh@Jimmy on 4 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/7861144/
8 but cannot prove how the accident occurred.

annotations.text: The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record.
The Act itself contains a provision which concerns with the consequences of driving dangerously alike the provision in the IPC that the vehicle is driven in a manner dangerous to public life.
Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act.
The courts have also taken the concept of 'culpable rashness' and 'culpable negligence' into consideration in cases of road accidents.

'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).

'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.

This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct.
[Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988' (First Edition, 2010]."
21. Rash or negligent driving has to be seen from the attendant circumstances.
The only question to be seen is whether the said injuries were caused by the reckless and negligent driving of the accused.

15. In order to establish an offence punishable under Section 279 of the IPC, it must be shown that the accused was driving the vehicle on a public road in a rash or negligent way, threatening human life or likely to cause harm or injury to another person.
Therefore, the main ingredients which need to be established beyond reasonable doubt by the prosecution are:
a) Firstly, that the accused was driving the vehicle on a public road;
b) Secondly, that the accused was driving the vehicle in a rash or negligent manner so as to endanger human life; and;
c) Thirdly, that death has been caused due to the said conduct of the accused.
However, the point of contention in the present case is whether the offending vehicle was being driven by the accused in a rash or negligent manner and that the accused caused the death of the victim due to such driving.
17. Therefore, the only question remaining to be proved by the prosecution is that the accused was driving the offending vehicle in a rash or negligent manner and that such driving has caused death of the victim.
summary.ANALYSIS:
Where an offence under Section 279 is established, the accused is also culpable under Section 304A of the IPC where his rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide causes death of any person.
Therefore, it is established that the victim passed away on account of the injuries which appear to have been suffered due to a road accident.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ravi Kapoor vs. State of Rajasthan [Crl. Appeal No.
1838/2009] inter alia held as under:
"10.
It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
It must be examined in light of the attendant circumstances.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.
Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to 'rash and negligent driving' within the meaning of the language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the legislature in its wisdom has used the words 'manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life'.
The preliminary conditions, thus, are that (a)
it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.

11. 'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.
Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one;
it is rather a comparative term.

Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.
In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence.
12. The Court has to adopt another parameter, i.e., 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.
The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrian happen to be children of tender years.
It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others.
The Act itself contains a provision which concerns with the consequences of driving dangerously alike the provision in the IPC that the vehicle is driven in a manner dangerous to public life.
Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act.
'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
There are no other public witnesses (who are not family members of the victim) who have been examined.
The site plan also does not confirm the version of the prosecution witnesses w.r.t. existence of a ramp.

The eye witnesses who ought to have established that the offending vehicle was being driven in a rash or negligent manner, have miserably failed to do so.

There is an absolute dearth of evidence regarding rashness or negligence in the manner in which the accused was driving the vehicle as the deposition of public witnesses qua said fact is absent.

Some credible and reliable evidence is indispensably needed to presume that the victim was behaving prudently while the accused acted negligently while driving the offending vehicle.
